## Eight common assumptions, negated

1. **Alpha is batch-independent.**
   - *Negation:* In the sklearn convention, the L2 term is divided by the minibatch size, and small batches take more steps per epoch. Per-epoch decay therefore scales roughly with 1/batch.
   - *Consequence:* Alpha-up hurts more at small batches, and batch-up helps more when alpha is high.
2. **L2 cost is independent of architecture size.**
   - *Negation:* The penalty sums over parameters and compounds multiplicatively through layers.
   - *Consequence:* Alpha-up hurts deep stacks more. Wide, overparameterized nets may benefit instead.
3. **The best learning rate does not depend on width.**
   - *Negation:* The best learning rate shrinks with width, in line with standard-parameterization and muP reasoning.
   - *Consequence:* Width-up hurts at high LR and helps at low LR. LR-up is safer in narrow nets.
4. **Depth helps or hurts the same way at any width.**
   - *Negation:* Narrow layers act as information bottlenecks.
   - *Consequence:* Depth-up hurts at narrow width and helps at wide width.
5. **243 epochs is enough to converge regardless of batch size.**
   - *Negation:* Large batches give too few updates for deep nets or small learning rates.
   - *Consequence:* Depth-up and batch-up are worse when the step budget is already tight.
6. **Learning rate and batch size are separable.**
   - *Negation:* Gradient noise scale couples them.
   - *Consequence:* LR-up is harmful at tiny batches, and batch-up is harmful at low LR.
7. **Capacity routes add up.**
   - *Negation:* Width and depth substitute for each other.
   - *Consequence:* Width-up matters most when depth is 1.
8. **Under Adam, regularization and optimization are orthogonal.**
   - *Negation:* With coupled L2 in Adam, a strong penalty dominates the normalized gradient.
   - *Consequence:* The value of a larger LR changes when alpha is high, and the value of width or depth changes when alpha is near zero.

## Hypotheses (summarised)

|---|------|-----------|------------|----------------|
| 1 | alpha up | batch_size low | lower | Decay per epoch ∝ 1/batch |
| 2 | alpha up | batch_size high | higher | Decay per epoch ∝ 1/batch |
| 3 | batch_size up | alpha high | higher | Larger batch relieves over-strong decay |
| 4 | alpha up | width high | higher | Overparameterization favours regularization |
| 5 | alpha up | depth high | lower | Penalty compounds across layers |
| 6 | width up | learning_rate_init high | lower | Best LR shrinks with width |
| 7 | width up | learning_rate_init low | higher | Wider nets make faster progress at low LR |
| 8 | depth up | width low | lower | Narrow layers bottleneck |
| 9 | depth up | width high | higher | Wide layers make extra depth usable |
| 10 | depth up | batch_size high | lower | Too few updates for deeper nets |
| 11 | depth up | learning_rate_init high | lower | Instability compounds with depth |
| 12 | learning_rate_init up | depth high | lower | Deep nets tolerate high LR poorly |
| 13 | learning_rate_init up | batch_size low | lower | Gradient noise times step size |
| 14 | batch_size up | learning_rate_init low | lower | Fewer steps with small LR, so underfitting |
| 15 | learning_rate_init up | alpha high | higher | Larger steps escape the penalty-dominated region |
| 16 | width up | alpha low | lower | Unregularized width overfits small datasets |
| 17 | width up | depth low | higher | Width is the only capacity route at depth 1 |
| 18 | depth up | alpha low | higher | Little compounded penalty on deep stacks |
| 19 | batch_size up | depth low | higher | Shallow nets need fewer updates |
| 20 | learning_rate_init up | width low | higher | Narrow nets tolerate larger LR |
